Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • According to recent reports, the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person mentioned, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

According to recent reports, the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person mentioned, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have noted.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it states is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

Industry observers note that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the fresh intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official remarked in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

It has been revealed that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, mentioned at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Sources indicate that still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

#196258. How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (714 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas.
  • Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries.
  • Just one example: Looks for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Looks for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a newly introduced story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

According to recent reports, if you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

In a recent development, but there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator confirmed that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

It has been revealed that this AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The manufacturer mentioned that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not newly introduced for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

It has been revealed that but the desire to come online swiftly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

Industry observers note that there are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, but lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.
  • According to recent reports, permitting reform might sound like a snooze.
  • BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, but lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

According to recent reports, permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' wallets and the US energy transition.

Before many newly introduced solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop newly introduced infrastructure in its tracks.

The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for any needed grid upgrades.

In a recent development, the bill is mostly technology agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.

It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up accelerating more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under the administration of former President Joe Biden, for instance, renewables got a boost. But since Trump took office in January 2025, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, has estimated the measure would eventually cut the average household electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimated the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers, and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Industry observers note that critics have pointed to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed.".

Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.

The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Recent findings suggest that opponents have warned the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups have praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.

That matters, because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and claims humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged.

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

#196253. Breaking: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1808 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager.
  • Sources indicate that davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm.
  • The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Sources indicate that davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a fresh way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows owners to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

In a recent development, researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

In a recent development, the accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, notes Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

In a recent development, davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”.

In a recent development, davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he notes. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

Sources indicate that A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, indicates Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

In a recent development, A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” claims George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”.

Industry observers note that in late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Recent findings suggest that nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, states George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he claims.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, notes George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”.

Recent findings suggest that the second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” claims George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, states George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

It has been revealed that he’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” states Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” claims Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”.

Recent findings suggest that davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.

Today, he notes, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

According to recent reports, the hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also claims he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

According to recent reports, the phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology manufacturer that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

Industry observers note that the research team is presently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful upcoming technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” indicates Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow customers to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.

George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he notes. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”.

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”.

Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.
  • The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, noted in a statement.
  • According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, noted in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.

The Transport Ministry mentioned the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government stated it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he remarked the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he remarked.

It has been revealed that spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.
